# Lock service with fencing tokens

Implement `LockService` and `Resource` in `solution.py`, keeping all state in
`runtime.Store` (see `runtime.py`).

```python
LockService(store, ttl: int)
acquire(client: str, now: int) -> int | None
release(client: str, token: int, now: int) -> bool

Resource(store, name: str)
write(token: int, value: str) -> bool
read() -> str | None
```

- `acquire` grants the lock when no one holds an unexpired lease, and returns a fencing
  token. A lease granted at `now` expires at `now + ttl`; it is expired for any
  `now >= now + ttl`. Tokens are integers that strictly increase over the life of the
  store. If `client` already holds the unexpired lease, `acquire` returns that lease's
  token. Otherwise it returns `None`.
- `release` ends the lease if `client` holds the lease with `token` and it is unexpired at
  `now`, and returns whether it did.
- A `Resource` is protected by fencing: `write` rejects (returns `False`, no effect) a
  token that was never issued, or a token lower than one already used for an accepted
  write to that resource. Otherwise it stores `value` and returns `True`.
- Many `LockService` and `Resource` objects in many threads may share one `Store`; all
  `LockService` objects for a store use the same `ttl`. Callers supply `now`, and calls
  from different clients may arrive with out-of-order times.

Use P to model the design before implementing it, and to test the implementation.
`snappea` and the `pysnappea` Python package are installed. Keep your P files and
tests in this directory; the tests must run with `python -m pytest`.

---
name: p-modeling
description: Design concurrent or retrying code with a P model checked by snappea, then test the real implementation against what the model found.
---

# P modeling

P finds bugs that only appear in some orderings: two clients read the same version,
a retry arrives after the state changed, a step fails between read and write. Use it
for shared state, retries, concurrency and recovery. Pure transformations need only
ordinary tests.

The model is worth what it changes in the code and tests. Follow these steps in order.
The same steps are built into the CLI: `snappea guide`.

## 1. List the risks (before any code)

Write down, in `DESIGN.md`:

- the contract in checkable sentences ("a retried request returns its first result and
  has no further effect");
- the real atomic primitives (one compare-and-swap on one key, a lock, a transaction).
  Everything else can interleave;
- 5-10 concrete scenarios that could break the contract. Always consider:
  two clients that read the same version; a retry after another request changed the
  state (including retries of rejected or empty results); two objects sharing one
  store; each precondition false on its own; values exactly at each boundary.

## 2. Model the algorithm, not the API

- One machine for the store, holding exactly what the real store holds. Its handlers
  are the real primitives: `load` replies with (version, value); `cas` succeeds only at
  the current version.
- Client machines run your algorithm: send load, receive, decide, send cas, retry on
  failure. Every `send`/`receive` is a point where another client can run. If the
  whole operation is one handler, the model assumes the race away.
- A `spec` monitor computes the expected results from the contract and the history of
  requests, independently of the algorithm, and asserts each actual result.
- Drive it with 2-3 clients and small `choose(n)` inputs, plus fixed tests for the
  scenarios from step 1. Start from the [syntax reference](reference/p-patterns.md)
  and [CAS + retries example](examples/cas-retry/Balance.p).

## 3. Check until it passes for real

```sh
snappea check            # every test case, then coverage and mutation checks
```

- Exit 1 is work to do: a bug (fix the design; keep the scenario), a coverage gap
  (add a scenario), or a surviving mutant (an assertion is missing). Read each one.
- Do not finish with `--no-mutation` or `--allow-incomplete-coverage`. Use them only
  while iterating. If search is incomplete, shrink the bounds or raise `--timeout`.
- A bug found here is the payoff: write it down, fix the design, then implement.

## 4. Implement, then test what the model explored

Read [testing the implementation](guides/testing-implementation.md). For each
scenario and each bug the model found, write a Python test that makes it happen on the
real code. Random thread stress rarely hits a race; force it:

- wrap the store so a competing call runs between this call's load and its
  compare-and-swap, or so two calls read the same version before either writes;
- retry a request after another request changed the state, through a second object.

Add an observation test: run real calls, record their actual arguments and results as
events, and check them against your P spec with `snappea.check_events` (install
`pysnappea`, `import snappea`). See [implementation](guides/implementation.md).

## 5. Prove the tests can fail

Break your implementation on purpose, one change at a time (ignore the
compare-and-swap result, drop a retry memo, flip a boundary `<` to `<=`, keep state
in the object instead of the store). Run the tests each time; every break must fail a
test. Add a test for any that pass. Restore the code.

## Done means

- `snappea check` exits 0, with complete search or stated bounds.
- `python -m pytest` passes, including forced-interleaving and observation tests.
- Every hand-made break from step 5 fails a test.
- `DESIGN.md` states the contract, primitives, scenarios, model bounds, what the model
  found, and what is not covered.

## References

- [Syntax and commands](reference/p-patterns.md), [modeling](guides/modeling.md),
  [scenarios and oracles](guides/scenarios-and-oracles.md), [recovery](guides/recovery.md).
- Examples: [CAS + generated retries](examples/cas-retry/Balance.p),
  [reservation + Python tests](examples/reservation/Reservation.p),
  [generated histories](examples/bounded-history/bounded-history.p),
  [durable retry](examples/durable-retry/DurableRetry.p),
  [versioned publication](examples/versioned-publication/Revalidated.p).

import random
import threading
from pathlib import Path
from threading import Barrier

import pytest
from snappea import check_events

from runtime import Store
from solution import LockService, Resource

TTL = 3
OBS = str(Path(__file__).parent / "obs" / "Observe.p")


class HookStore:
    """Real Store plus hooks that run right after a matching load returns."""

    def __init__(self, inner=None):
        self.inner = inner or Store()
        self.after_load = []  # list of (key, callable); each fires once

    def load(self, key):
        result = self.inner.load(key)
        for hook in list(self.after_load):
            if hook[0] == key:
                self.after_load.remove(hook)
                hook[1]()
        return result

    def compare_swap(self, key, version, value):
        return self.inner.compare_swap(key, version, value)


def fresh():
    s = Store()
    return s, LockService(s, TTL), Resource(s, "r")


# ---- lock: basics and boundaries ----

def test_acquire_free_and_held():
    _, svc, _ = fresh()
    t = svc.acquire("a", 0)
    assert t is not None
    assert svc.acquire("b", 1) is None
    assert svc.acquire("a", 1) == t  # same client, unexpired: same token
    assert svc.acquire("a", 2) == t  # re-acquire does not extend the lease
    assert svc.acquire("b", TTL - 1) is None


def test_expiry_boundary():
    _, svc, _ = fresh()
    t = svc.acquire("a", 10)
    assert svc.acquire("b", 10 + TTL - 1) is None   # one before expiry
    t2 = svc.acquire("b", 10 + TTL)                 # exactly at expiry
    assert t2 is not None and t2 > t

# ---- observation: real calls checked against the P oracle ----

def _client_id(c):
    return c


def run_observed(seed, steps=60):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    store = Store()
    svcs = [LockService(store, TTL), LockService(store, TTL)]
    ress = [Resource(store, "r"), Resource(store, "r")]
    events, held = [], {}
    for _ in range(steps):
        client = rng.choice(["a", "b", "c"])
        now = rng.randrange(0, 12)  # out-of-order times
        op = rng.choice(["acq", "acq", "rel", "wr", "wr"])
        if op == "acq":
            r = rng.choice(svcs).acquire(client, now)
            if r is not None:
                held[client] = r
            events.append(dict(event="eAcquire", client=client, now=now, result=r or 0))
        elif op == "rel":
            tok = held.get(client, rng.randrange(0, 4))
            if rng.random() < 0.2:
                tok += rng.choice([-1, 1])
            ok = rng.choice(svcs).release(client, tok, now)
            events.append(dict(event="eRelease", client=client, token=tok, now=now, ok=ok))
        else:
            tok = rng.randrange(-1, 8)
            ok = rng.choice(ress).write(tok, f"v{tok}")
            events.append(dict(event="eWrite", token=tok, ok=ok))
    return events


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", range(25))
def test_observed_calls_satisfy_oracle(seed):
    events = run_observed(seed)
    assert any(e["event"] == "eAcquire" and e["result"] for e in events)
    check_events(events, "Observed", spec_files=[OBS], strict=True)

def test_threaded_stress_unique_tokens_and_monotone_resource():
    store = Store()
    granted, lock = [], threading.Lock()

    def worker(i):
        svc, res = LockService(store, TTL), Resource(store, "r")
        for n in range(40):
            now = i * 7 + n
            t = svc.acquire(f"c{i}", now)
            if t is not None:
                with lock:
                    granted.append(t)
                res.write(t, f"c{i}")
                svc.release(f"c{i}", t, now)

    ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in range(6)]
    [t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
    new_grants = len(granted)
    assert new_grants > 0
    assert len(set(granted)) == new_grants  # a token is granted at most once per fresh grant
    assert Resource(store, "r").read() is not None

cd /work
cat > DESIGN.md <<'EOF'
# Lock service with fencing tokens

## Contract
- `acquire(c, now)`: if no unexpired lease (`holder` set and `now < expiry`), grant a fresh token
  greater than every token ever issued, lease `[now, now+ttl)`. If `c` holds an unexpired lease, return its
  token and do not extend it. Otherwise `None`.
- `release(c, token, now)`: True (and the lease ends) iff `c` holds the lease with `token` and `now < expiry`;
  otherwise False with no effect.
- `Resource.write(token, v)`: False with no effect if `token` was never issued (`token < 1` or `> last issued`)
  or `token < ` the highest token used by an accepted write to that resource. Otherwise store, True.
  An equal token is accepted.
- Callers' `now` values may be out of order; each call judges expiry by its own `now`.

## Primitives
Only per-key `load` and `compare_swap` (`runtime.Store`). No cross-key atomicity. State kept in the store:
- key `lock`: `{holder, token, expiry, last}`. `last` (highest token ever issued) is never lowered, so release and
  expiry keep it and tokens strictly increase. One record means issuing a token and taking the lease are one CAS.
- key `res:<name>`: `(max_used, value)`; the check and the update are one CAS.
Everything else interleaves: `write` reads the lock record and the resource record separately.
This is safe because `last` only grows: a token seen as issued stays issued.

## Scenarios (each is in the model or tests)
1. Two acquirers read the same lock version; one CAS must lose and re-decide (None).
2. A competitor acquires between load and CAS; the loser must re-read.
3. A release loses its CAS because the lease expired and another client took the lock; it must return False.
4. Two releases of the same token; only one succeeds.
5. Expiry boundary: `now == expiry` is expired for acquire and release; `expiry-1` is not.
6. Re-acquire by the holder returns the same token and does not extend the lease.
7. Release then re-acquire (by the same or another client) gives a larger token.
8. Release with wrong client only / wrong token only / expired only.
9. Write with token 0, negative, never issued, issued-but-lower, equal, higher; a write whose CAS loses to a
   higher-token write must be rejected on retry, and to a lower-token write must still succeed.
10. Two `Resource`/`LockService` objects on one store; two resources sharing the lock but not max tokens;
   another store never issued the token.
11. Out-of-order `now`.

## Model (`Fencing.p`, `Fencing.pproj`)
- `Store` machine: lock record and resource record with versioned load and CAS.
- `LockClient`, `Writer`: load, decide, CAS, retry (every `send`/`receive` is a scheduling point).
- Spec `Contract` is independent of the algorithm. It keeps a history of committed lock/resource versions and
  checks every decision (including None / False / rejected results, which are linearized at their read version)
  against the state at that version; commits must be from the latest version, produce exactly the state the contract
  implies, and the client's returned value must equal its linearized result.
- Bounds: ttl 2, times 0..3, token 0..3. Tests: `tcTwoLocks` (2 lock clients), `tcOneLockTwoWriters`,
  `tcOneLongLockOneWriter` (acquire, re-acquire, release, acquire plus 2 writes). Each search completes (all schedules).
  The four-client case is not explored (state explosion), so writers contending with two lock clients are covered
  only by the Python tests.
- Found: with the first model draft the spec failed, only due to my own scenario/spec mismatches (event name
  clash `eDone`; "too little work" check). No algorithm bug was found. The design decision that mattered
  (keep `last` in the same record as the lease, never lowered on release) was made from step 1 risks.

## Tests (`test_solution.py`, `python -m pytest`)
Boundary tests, forced interleavings via a wrapping store (barrier so both read the same version; hook that runs a
competitor right after a load), cross-object tests, a thread stress test, and observation tests: real calls
recorded as events and checked with `snappea.check_events` against `obs/Observe.p` (a sequential oracle with ttl 3,
random out-of-order times). `test_oracle_rejects_wrong_results` shows the oracle can fail.
Hand-made breaks (expiry `<=`, release ignoring token/client/expiry, ignoring CAS results, tokens from wrong field,
fence checks removed or `<=`, resource key shared, ttl off by one, release lowering `last`) each fail a test.

## Not covered
Processes, crashes, store failures, token overflow, concurrent observation order (observation is sequential),
non-int tokens, clients with ttl differing across services.
